summary: UK airspace is the London and Scottish FIRs (surface to FL245). Classes A to E are controlled; F and G are not. Control Zones start at the surface; Control Areas, TMAs and airways start at a base. Class A is closed to VFR, B and F are unused, most CTRs are D, and everything above FL195 is C. ATZs run from the surface to 2,000 ft aal with a 2 or 2.5 nm radius; MATZs to 3,000 ft aal and 5 nm, with 4 nm by 5 nm stubs. Special VFR lets you fly in a CTR below VMC. Know how Danger Areas are drawn and labelled, and the hazards that live in Class G.
sections: Flight Information Regions
UK airspace has two Flight Information Regions: London and Scottish
The FIRs run from the surface to FL245. Above that is upper airspace: the London and Scottish UIRs, FL245 to FL660 (in Europe the UIR starts at FL195)
On the 1:500,000 chart the boundary is labelled SCOTTISH FIR EGPX / LONDON FIR EGTT, near 55°N in the east
Airspace is subdivided by the amount and type of flying: tightly regulated round London, little regulation over the Outer Hebrides
Controlled and uncontrolled airspace
Two categories: controlled and uncontrolled
ICAO classes A to G: A is the busiest controlled airspace; B, C, D and E are other controlled airspace; F and G are uncontrolled
Each class has its own VMC minima and level of air traffic service
In controlled airspace ATC is provided to all flights. UK controlled airspace is made of CTRs, TMAs, CTAs and Airways
Class A is closed to VFR and Class B is not used in the UK, so UK VFR in controlled airspace is usually in C, D or E
Control Zones, TMAs, CTAs and Airways

Control Zone (CTR): around certain aerodromes, from the surface to a specified altitude or FL; at least 5 nm either side of the aerodrome centre along the approach path. Most UK CTRs are Class D (even Heathrow)
Control Area (CTA): controlled airspace from a specified base up to an upper limit. UK CTAs are Class A, C or D

Terminal Control Area (TMA): a CTA at the confluence of ATS routes near one or more major aerodromes. Four in the UK: London, Manchester, Scottish, Belfast (Class A, C, D or E). TCA is another abbreviation; TMA comes from Terminal Manoeuvring Area
Airway: a CTA shaped as a corridor, 5 nm each side of the centreline, with set vertical limits, e.g. A25 (Alpha Two Five), R8 (Romeo Eight). Class A, E or C. The base steps down near aerodromes
Trap: surface upwards = Control Zone; from a base upwards = Control Area
Controlled airspace on charts
1:500,000 chart: controlled airspace up to FL195, with its class
1:250,000 chart: all controlled airspace with a base at or below 3,000 ft amsl
Class D boundaries are blue dashed lines. A + after a limit (e.g. FL55+) means up to FL195

Examples: Leeds Bradford CTR, Class D, surface to FL85; London TMA, Class A, 5,500 ft to FL195; Southampton CTR, Class D, surface to 2,000 ft; Solent CTA, Class D, 2,000 ft to FL55; Airway R37, Class A, FL115 to FL195
Full descriptions in AIP ENR; Pooley's lists controlling units and frequencies
Special VFR
Special VFR (SERA.5010): an ATC authorisation to fly in a Control Zone in weather below VMC without full IFR
Stay clear of cloud and in sight of the surface; you are responsible for obstacle clearance
Flight visibility at least 1,500 m; speed 140 kt or less
No take-off, landing, or entering the ATZ or circuit if the reported ground visibility is below 1,500 m or the cloud ceiling below 600 ft

Under ATC instruction the 1,000 ft congested-area rule may be relaxed, but you must be able to glide clear, stay 500 ft from people, vessels, vehicles and structures, and land only at a licensed or Government aerodrome (unless the CAA agrees)
Only in Control Zones. May be requested to transit a Class A CTR (none in the UK), never other Class A
No flight plan needed, but ATC approval is. ATC separate you from other SVFR and IFR traffic; their instructions must be followed
Crossing an airway
A pilot without an IMC or instrument rating may fly at right angles across the base of an en-route airway whose lower limit is a flight level, in VMC, but must not enter it
E.g. Airway B1, base FL75: cross beneath it, north or south, not above FL75

With a valid Instrument Rating you may cross through an airway in VMC by day if you file a flight plan and request a crossing clearance at least 10 minutes before the crossing point, and receive it before crossing
Cross by the shortest route (normally at right angles), in level flight at the cleared level
Uncontrolled airspace: the Open-FIR
Class G, the Open-FIR, is about 50% of UK airspace and includes MATZs and the ATZs outside controlled airspace

FIS is available from London Information and Scottish Information (e.g. 124.75 MHz in the south-west): weather, nav aid serviceability, aerodrome conditions, alerting, proximity warnings and other advisory information
Radar services (Traffic or Deconfliction) from ATSUs, including LARS units
ATZs and MATZs have their own frequencies
Flight in an ATZ is regulated by Rule 11, so ATZs, like controlled airspace, are regulated airspace
Aerodrome Traffic Zones (ATZ)
At most UK civil and military aerodromes. An ATZ has no class of its own: it takes the class of the airspace it is in
From the surface to 2,000 ft aal, a circle centred on the mid-point of the longest runway
Radius 2 nm if the longest runway is 1,850 m or less; 2.5 nm if it is longer
Some 2 nm ATZs are enlarged to 2.5 nm to give at least 1.5 nm beyond every runway end
Listed in AIP AD 2 and on 1:500,000 and 1:250,000 charts, plus an ATZ list on the 1:500,000. ATZs wholly inside regulated airspace (e.g. Birmingham) are not drawn on the 1:500,000
Rule 11: flying in an ATZ
Do not fly in an ATZ unless you have permission from ATC; or, with no ATC, enough information from the AFIS unit; or, with neither, enough information from the A/G radio station
Keep a continuous watch on the frequency (or watch for visual signals)
With a radio, report position and height on entering and leaving, and make any other standard or requested calls
Applies at a Government aerodrome at notified times (usually H24); at an aerodrome with ATC or AFIS during its hours of watch; at a licensed aerodrome with A/G radio during its notified hours
If the ATZ is inside stricter airspace (e.g. Class D), the stricter rules apply
Trap: the report is position and height, not heading or intentions
Military Aerodrome Traffic Zones (MATZ)
Surface to 3,000 ft aal, radius 5 nm
Usually one or more stubs along the final approach of the main instrument runway(s): 4 nm wide, extending a further 5 nm, from 1,000 ft to 3,000 ft aal
Civil pilots are strongly advised to enter under the control of the MATZ unit (AIP ENR 2.2, Pooley's)
A MATZ is not regulated airspace, but the ATZ inside it must always be observed (most are H24)
UK airspace classes
Class A: airways, London and Manchester TMAs, Cotswold, Daventry and Worthing CTAs. No VFR
Class B: not allocated in the UK
Class C: all airspace above FL195, plus some CTAs below it (e.g. Daventry 21 and 22, Severn 1 and 2, Clacton 10-12)
Class D: less busy airspace: most CTRs and CTAs, the Scottish TMA, and ATZs inside Class D CTRs
Class E: below FL195, e.g. parts of the Scottish TMA below 6,000 ft, parts of the Farnborough CTA, Doncaster Sheffield CTA 13, Holyhead CTAs 15 and 16, Argyll and Moray CTAs, some airways
Class F: not allocated in the UK. Class G: everything else (the Open-FIR)
VFR in Class C and D needs flight notification and an ATC clearance
Prohibited, Restricted and Danger Areas
Prohibited Area: flight is prohibited (e.g. P611/2.2, surface to 2,200 ft)
Restricted Area: flight is restricted according to certain conditions
Danger Area: activities dangerous to flight may happen (AIP ENR 5). Solid red outline: active in published hours. Pecked red: inactive unless notified by NOTAM

Reading D129/1.75: the first digit is the latitude band (1 = between 51°N and 52°N); after the slash, the upper limit in thousands of ft amsl (1,750 ft, from the surface). "1-2.5" would be 1,000 to 2,500 ft amsl
An asterisk (*) means by-laws prohibit entry while the area is active
DACS (Danger Area Crossing Service) and DAAIS (Danger Area Activity Information Service) are listed on the 1:500,000 chart
Weapon Range Danger Areas: get a radar service near them. Pilotless aircraft (orange or red, up to 60,000 ft, mainly West Wales): avoid the recovery part of their areas
All of these are on the AIP's Chart of UK Airspace Restrictions and Hazardous Areas; changes by NOTAM and AIC
Obstructions
Structures 100 m agl or more are in AIP ENR 5.4 and on certain charts
Beyond 15 km of an aerodrome, obstacles over 150 m are en-route obstacles: steady red lights at night, some with high-intensity flashing white lights
Obstructions may or may not be lit; windfarms are often unlit. Charts show amsl with agl in brackets, e.g. 840 (380)
Aerodrome obstructions: AIP AD and instrument approach charts
Other hazards
Winch-launched gliders: cable up to 2,000 ft agl (higher at a few sites). Aerotow: glider and tug joined by up to 150 m of cable
Parachute training balloons: no notification; up to 1,000 ft agl, in visibility of 5 km or more and 1,000 ft from cloud
Parachuting: free-fall up to FL150; expect parachutists within 1.5 nm of the drop zone. Also by day at any Government or licensed aerodrome
Parascending and hang-gliders: up to cloud base or the base of controlled airspace (whichever is lower); cables to 2,000 ft agl
Military low flying up to 2,000 ft agl, busiest 250 to 500 ft agl: avoid that band. Avoid AIAAs if you can
Gas venting sites: severe turbulence; magenta circle with the hazard altitude. Small arms ranges: hazard below 500 ft agl, not Danger Areas
Target towing: up to 2,000 ft of cable, by day in VMC, up to 10,000 ft
Birds: keep above the effective altitude over sanctuaries and above 1,500 ft agl over other concentrations. Strike risk rises with speed
HIRTA (High Intensity Radio Transmission Areas): interference with radios and nav equipment; some can endanger health
Royal Flights
A Royal Flight carries members of the Royal Family (others such as heads of state may get the status)
Fixed-wing: where possible within the normal route structure; otherwise temporary Class D controlled airspace, CAS-T, notified by NOTAM
Enter CAS-T only with an ATC clearance, whatever the weather
Temporary Control Zones: radius 5 to 10 nm, active from 15 minutes before to 30 minutes after ETD and ETA. Temporary airways: 5 nm each side of track
Helicopters: no CAS-T normally; a Royal Low-Level Corridor is notified by NOTAM

sum.Flight Information Regions: London and Scottish FIRs, surface to FL245; UIRs above.
sum.Controlled and uncontrolled airspace: A to E controlled, F and G uncontrolled; UK VFR usually in C, D, E.
sum.Control Zones, TMAs, CTAs and Airways: CTR from the surface; CTA, TMA and airways from a base. Airways 5 nm each side.
sum.Controlled airspace on charts: Half-million to FL195; quarter-million for bases at or below 3,000 ft.
sum.Special VFR: In a CTR below VMC: clear of cloud, sight of surface, 1,500 m, 140 kt; ATC approval, no flight plan.
sum.Crossing an airway: Without an IR, only beneath a FL base at right angles; with an IR, clearance 10 minutes ahead.
sum.Uncontrolled airspace: the Open-FIR: Class G, about half the UK; FIS from London or Scottish Information.
sum.Aerodrome Traffic Zones (ATZ): Surface to 2,000 ft aal; 2 nm (runway up to 1,850 m) or 2.5 nm.
sum.Rule 11: flying in an ATZ: Permission from ATC or information from AFIS or A/G; listen out; report position and height.
sum.Military Aerodrome Traffic Zones (MATZ): Surface to 3,000 ft aal, 5 nm; stubs 4 nm wide, 5 nm long, 1,000 to 3,000 ft.
sum.UK airspace classes: A: no VFR; B and F unused; C above FL195; D most CTRs; G the rest.
sum.Prohibited, Restricted and Danger Areas: Solid red active, pecked red only by NOTAM; D129/1.75 decoded.
sum.Obstructions: 100 m agl and over listed; en-route obstacles lit red.
sum.Other hazards: Cables to 2,000 ft, parachuting to FL150, low flying 250-500 ft, birds below 1,500 ft.
sum.Royal Flights: Temporary Class D (CAS-T) by NOTAM; clearance needed.

cards.q: Vertical extent of the UK FIRs?

cards.a: A, B, C, D and E.

cards.q: Which UK classes can VFR flights use in controlled airspace?
cards.a: Usually C, D and E (A is closed to VFR; B is not used).

cards.q: 1:500,000 chart shows controlled airspace up to?
1:250,000 chart shows controlled airspace with a base at or below?
SVFR: no take-off or landing if ground visibility is below / ceiling below?

cards.a: Not required, but ATC approval is.

cards.q: Crossing an airway without an instrument rating?
cards.a: Only beneath its base (where the base is a FL), at right angles, in VMC.

cards.q: Airway crossing with an IR: how early to request clearance?
cards.a: At least 10 minutes before the crossing point.

cards.q: Share of UK airspace that is Class G?
ATZ radius, longest runway 1,850 m or less?
ATZ radius, longest runway over 1,850 m?

cards.a: The mid-point of the longest runway.
None of its own: it takes the class of the surrounding airspace.
Position and height, entering and leaving.

cards.q: Rule 11 with no ATC or AFIS?
cards.a: Get enough information from the A/G station to fly safely.
Surface to 3,000 ft aal, 5 nm radius.
4 nm wide, 5 nm long, 1,000 to 3,000 ft aal.
No, but the ATZ inside it is.
All airspace above FL195, plus certain CTAs.

cards.q: Asterisk before a Danger Area number?

cards.a: Up to FL150, within 1.5 nm of the drop zone.
1,500 ft agl (above the effective altitude over sanctuaries).

cards.q: Structures listed as air navigation obstructions?

cards.a: CAS-T, Class D, notified by NOTAM; enter only with a clearance.

quiz.q: A Danger Area on the 1:500,000 chart has a pecked red outline. It is:
o: Inactive unless notified by NOTAM
Active only in its published hours
Always active, day and night
Inactive in daylight, active at night
quiz.why: Pecked = inactive unless NOTAMed. A solid red outline is active in its published hours.

quiz.q: Controlled airspace from the surface to a specified upper limit is a:
o: Control Zone
Control Area
Aerodrome Traffic Zone
Airway
quiz.why: Surface upwards is a CTR. A CTA (and an airway) starts at a base above the surface; an ATZ is not controlled airspace in itself.

ref.sec: Control Zones, TMAs, CTAs and Airways

quiz.q: A Terminal Control Area is:
o: A Control Area at the confluence of ATS routes near one or more major aerodromes
A Control Zone at the confluence of ATS routes near one or more major aerodromes
A Control Area for arriving flights only
A Control Area for departing flights only
quiz.why: It is a Control Area (it has a base), not a Control Zone. It serves both arrivals and departures.

ref.sec: Control Zones, TMAs, CTAs and Airways

quiz.q: "P611/2.2" on a chart is:
o: A Prohibited Area, surface to 2,200 ft
A Danger Area, surface to 2,200 ft
A Restricted Area, surface to 2,200 ft
A Prohibited Area, surface to 22,000 ft
quiz.why: P is Prohibited; 2.2 is the upper limit in thousands of feet: 2,200 ft.

quiz.q: The dimensions of a MATZ stub are:
o: 1,000 to 3,000 ft aal, 4 nm wide, extending 5 nm
1,000 to 3,000 ft aal, 5 nm wide, extending 4 nm
2,000 to 3,000 ft aal, 4 nm wide, extending 5 nm
1,000 to 2,000 ft aal, 5 nm wide, extending 4 nm
quiz.why: Stubs: 4 nm wide, 5 nm long, from 1,000 to 3,000 ft aal. The traps swap the 4 and the 5.

quiz.q: An aerodrome's longest runway is 2,000 m. Its ATZ is:
o: 2.5 nm radius, surface to 2,000 ft aal
2 nm radius, surface to 2,000 ft aal
5 nm radius, surface to 3,000 ft aal
2.5 km radius, surface to 2,000 ft aal
quiz.why: Over 1,850 m gives 2.5 nm (nautical miles, not km). 5 nm and 3,000 ft are MATZ figures.

quiz.q: Flying in an ATZ with a radio, you must:
o: Keep a continuous listening watch and report position and height entering and leaving
Keep a continuous listening watch and report position and heading entering and leaving
Keep a continuous listening watch and report position and intentions entering and leaving
Report position and height entering and leaving, without a listening watch in between
quiz.why: Position and height, plus a continuous watch. Heading and intentions are the distractors.

quiz.q: A Special VFR flight is:
o: A VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate in a Control Zone in conditions below VMC
A VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate in any controlled airspace in conditions below VMC
A VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate in a Control Area in conditions below VMC
A VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate in a Control Zone in conditions below IMC
quiz.why: SVFR exists only in Control Zones. 'Below IMC' is meaningless: SVFR is used below VMC.

quiz.q: Under SVFR, which minimum flight visibility applies?
o: 5 km
quiz.why: SVFR needs a flight visibility of at least 1,500 m, clear of cloud and in sight of the surface.

quiz.q: You may not take off under SVFR if the reported conditions at the aerodrome are:
o: Ground visibility below 1,500 m or cloud ceiling below 600 ft
Ground visibility below 1,500 m or cloud ceiling below 1,000 ft
Ground visibility below 5 km or cloud ceiling below 600 ft
Flight visibility below 1,500 m or cloud ceiling below 1,500 ft
quiz.why: The limits are ground visibility 1,500 m and ceiling 600 ft.

quiz.q: Which statement about SVFR is correct?
o: No flight plan is needed, but ATC approval is
A full flight plan must be filed
It can be used in any Class A airspace
It can be used in Class G outside a Control Zone
quiz.why: SVFR needs ATC approval but no flight plan. It exists only in Control Zones and never in Class A outside a CTR.

quiz.q: The speed limit under SVFR is:
o: 140 kt
250 kt
120 kt
100 kt
quiz.why: 140 kt. 250 kt is the speed limit below FL100 for VFR in some airspace classes.

quiz.q: Without an instrument rating, how may you cross an airway whose base is FL75?
o: Beneath it, at right angles, not above FL75, in VMC
Through it at FL80 in VMC, without a clearance
Through it in VMC, with a crossing clearance
Not at all without an instrument rating, even below it
quiz.why: You may pass under the base at right angles but must not enter. Entering needs an IR and a crossing clearance.

quiz.q: With an instrument rating, a crossing clearance for an airway should be requested at least:
o: 10 minutes before the crossing point
5 minutes before the crossing point
30 minutes before the crossing point
Before departure, when filing the flight plan
quiz.why: At least 10 minutes before, and the clearance must be received before crossing.

quiz.q: Which UK airspace class is NOT available to VFR flights?
o: Class A
Class C
Class D
Class E
quiz.why: Class A is IFR only. VFR may use C and D with a clearance, and E.

quiz.q: All UK airspace above FL195 is:
o: Class C
Class A
Class D
Class G
quiz.why: Above FL195 the London and Scottish FIR airspace is Class C.

quiz.q: Most UK Control Zones, including Heathrow's, are:
o: Class D
Class A
Class C
Class E
quiz.why: Most UK CTRs are Class D.

quiz.q: What class is an ATZ?
o: It has the class of the airspace around it
It is always Class D, whatever surrounds it
It is always Class G, wherever it is
It is always Class F advisory airspace
quiz.why: An ATZ has no class of its own.

quiz.q: Where is the centre of an ATZ?
o: The mid-point of the longest runway
The notified aerodrome reference point
The aerodrome control tower or radio room
The threshold of the main instrument runway
quiz.why: The circle is centred on the notified mid-point of the longest runway.

quiz.q: At an aerodrome with no ATC or AFIS, Rule 11 lets you fly in the ATZ if you have:
o: Enough information from the A/G radio station to fly safely
Permission from the A/G radio operator to fly within the ATZ
Permission from London Information to enter the ATZ
A clearance from the nearest ATC unit to enter the ATZ
quiz.why: A/G stations give information, not permission; ATC gives permission; AFIS gives information.

quiz.q: Where an ATZ lies within Class D airspace:
o: The stricter Class D rules apply
Only the ATZ rules apply
Neither applies to VFR flights
The pilot chooses which rules apply
quiz.why: The more stringent rules take precedence.

quiz.q: A Danger Area is labelled D129/1.75. It lies:
o: Between 51°N and 52°N, from the surface to 1,750 ft amsl
Between 52°N and 53°N, from the surface to 1,750 ft agl
Between 51°N and 52°N, from the surface to 17,500 ft amsl
At 12.9°E, from the surface to 1,750 ft amsl or FL17
quiz.why: The first digit is the latitude band (1 = 51 to 52°N); after the slash the top is in thousands of ft amsl.

quiz.q: An asterisk before a Danger Area number means:
o: By-laws prohibit entry while it is active
It is never active and can be ignored
A crossing service is available on request
It contains unmanned or pilotless aircraft
quiz.why: By-law areas may not be entered during their activity.

quiz.q: The 1:250,000 chart shows all controlled airspace with a base:
o: At or below 3,000 ft amsl
Up to FL195
At or below 5,000 ft amsl
Below FL100
quiz.why: The half-million shows up to FL195; the quarter-million shows everything with a base at or below 3,000 ft amsl.

quiz.q: Free-fall parachuting can be expected up to:
o: FL150, within 1.5 nm of the drop zone
FL100, within 1 nm of the drop zone
5,000 ft, within 2 nm of the drop zone
FL150, within 5 nm of the drop zone
quiz.why: Up to FL150 within a 1.5 nm radius of the DZ.

quiz.q: Winch-launched gliders may carry the cable up to about:
o: 2,000 ft agl
1,000 ft agl
3,000 ft agl
500 ft agl
quiz.why: 2,000 ft agl, and higher at a few sites.

quiz.q: Military low flying is concentrated between:
o: 250 and 500 ft agl
500 and 1,000 ft agl
1,000 and 2,000 ft agl
Surface and 250 ft agl
quiz.why: Low flying happens up to 2,000 ft agl but is busiest at 250 to 500 ft agl.

quiz.q: Over areas where birds concentrate (not sanctuaries) you should avoid flying below:
o: 1,500 ft agl
500 ft agl
1,000 ft agl
3,000 ft agl
quiz.why: Below 1,500 ft agl; over sanctuaries, keep above the listed effective altitude.

quiz.q: Is a MATZ regulated airspace?
o: No, but the ATZ within it must always be observed
Yes, always: entry needs a clearance at all times
Only when the military aerodrome is open for flying
Only for military aircraft; civil aircraft may ignore it
quiz.why: Entering under MATZ control is strongly advised, not required, but the ATZ inside applies (usually H24).

quiz.q: The upper limit of the UK FIRs is:
o: FL245
FL195
FL660
FL100
quiz.why: FIRs run from the surface to FL245; the UIRs from FL245 to FL660.

quiz.q: CAS-T for a Royal Flight is:
o: Temporary Class D airspace; enter only with an ATC clearance
Temporary Class A airspace, closed to all VFR flights
Advisory airspace you may enter freely, keeping a good lookout
A temporary Prohibited Area that no aircraft may enter
quiz.why: CAS-T is Class D and notified by NOTAM; you need a clearance whatever the weather.
